title: Davey says far right in Britain now better funded and supported than in the past – UK politics live
text:
Reform UK MSPs stage walkout from Scottish parliament after failing to block debate on independence
Turning away from the UN for a moment, Reform MSPs have staged a walkout from the Holyrood chamber after the party failed to get a debate on Scottish independence cancelled, the Press Association reports.
With first minister and SNP leader John Swinney having called a debate on Scotland’s right to decide, Malcolm Offord, the leader of Reform UK north of the border, insisted the issue of the constitution is a reserved matter and should not be discussed, PA says.
When his appeals to presiding officer Kenneth Gibson failed, Offord branded the debate a “farce” and led his MSPs in a walkout. Offord said:
This debate is not just a farce, it is an insult to the Scottish electorate who expect their politicians to deal with serious issues in their communities.
Offord argued that Scots want to see MSPs dealing with “shocking” homelessness figures released earlier on Tuesday, the nation’s public finances or drug deaths – with a further rise in these expected to be announced on Wednesday. He went on:
These are the serious matters of government.
In contrast this debate is ill-judged, self-serving and wholly inappropriate.
Reform won’t engage further in these pointless proceedings. We didn’t come into the parliament to waste our time on vanity projects, and therefore I withdraw my amendment and we will exit from the chamber.
MSPs were debating a motion from Swinney which declared: “Scotland is a nation that has a right to decide its own future.” It is set to be passed later.
We are now being told that the remarks from Andy Burnham and Donald Trump will come after they have had their meeting. Originally, they were expected to talk to the press before they went into their private session.
'Almost as silly as his photo stunts' - Reform UK and Tories claim Lib Dems' proposed £17bn tax cut not properly funded
Back to Ed Davey, and the Conservatives and Reform UK are both saying that Ed Davey’s proposed £17bn tax cut is not properly funded.
This is from Alex Burghart, the deputy Tory leader.
The Liberal Democrats are suffering from a bout of collective amnesia. Over the past two years they have aided and abetted Labour’s destruction of our economy. Now they are trying to shift the blame on to a vote that happened a decade ago.
Ed Davey has forgotten that you have to pay for access to the single market and customs union, giving up control both of your borders and your trade policy as well as your cash.
He wants to turn back the clock, taking us back to 2016. The Conservatives, in contrast, are focused on taking our country forward, and on getting Britain working again, including by setting out tax cuts that are actually costed.
And this is from Robert Jenrick, the Reform UK Treasury spokesperson.
Sir Ed is welcome to steal our policies, but his plan to pay for it is almost as silly as his photo stunts. At this rate, the Lib Dems’ fantasy economics would make Liz Truss blush.
The socks-and-sandals brigade would have to make the same choices we will: Cut the benefits bill, end net zero handouts, and slash foreign aid. But they refuse because they are incapable of putting the British people first.
In a briefing note about the plan to raise tax thresholds announced by Davey, the Liberal Democrats say:
The House of Commons Library estimates that this plan would cost £17bn in year five. This would be paid for by the dividends from the party’s plan for a new Growth and Defence Plan with Europe, which is estimated to be £27bn a year by the end of the next parliament.
This is fromPippa Crerar on Donald Trump’s speech to the UN, and where he differs from Andy Burnham on AI.
Trump vows to oppose any international regulation of AI – as proposed by Andy Burnham and separately by the Finns/ Norwegians.
US President says he wants to rename AI “super intelligence” because “artificial” suggests that it’s fake – and says he will win the AI race with China.
“We will only encourage super intelligence, not rein it in,” he says, adding that US has “never backed away from a frontier”.
But Andy Burnham is pushing for multilateral agreement on AI. He told a business event in NYC earlier:
“We want to pick up the initiatives that are beginning to emerge, develop, and bring them into a single set of global principles and standards that are very much about unlocking the full potential whilst guarding against the risks.”
Lucy Campbell has more on Trump’s speech on our US politics live blog.
Nature abhors a vacuum, a sage once said. (Which sage is a matter of dispute, but Rabelais, summing up Aristotle, is a common answer.) If it is true of nature, it is even more true of politics. The biggest gap in British politics at the moment is the one created by Kemi Badenoch when she became Tory leader and swerved her party to the right, leaving anyone with an allegiance to one nation, or pro-European, or moderate Conservatism essentially homeless.
Not anymore. With his speech today, Ed Davey did not just appeal to these voters (something he has been doing for a while). He came close to plonking his party on this territory.
There was little or nothing in the speech that someone like David Cameron or John Major would fundamentally disagree with. And while Davey used the word liberalism a lot (making a coherent argument linking Lib Dem community campaigning to respect for the “value of every human being”, and positing this as an antidote to far-right populism), he largely avoided the sort of internationalism or moral idealism you would have heard from predecessors like Paddy Ashdown, Charles Kennedy or Menzies Campbell. There was not much there about equality. And electoral reform – seen by many as the holy grail for liberal democracy – was more or less absent, apart from a cryptic reference to changing the nature of politics.
For the first time in postwar politics, Britain has a prime minister with a firm and apparently sincere commitment to PR. But, on the basis of this speech, you would assume that Davey was not particularly interested.
Instead, Davey’s big announcement was a tax cut – which is what you would expect from moderate Conservatism.
That does not mean it was a bad speech. It was clear, coherent, and well-argued; it was refreshingly free of naff jokes; and the references to his family were interesting and moving. The passage about how the politics of “hatred and intolerance” have always been defeated in the past was also inspiring.
For anyone who may have voted Conservative in 2024, but who finds Kemi Badenoch a bit extreme and who is horrified by the idea of Nigel Farage becoming PM – ie, key target voters for the Liberal Democrats – it would be very appealing.
But will Lib Dem activists like it? My colleague Peter Walker, who has been with them in Brighton this week, isn’t sure. He says:
Offering £17bn in tax cuts - even some time in the future - is certainly bold, but not sure it will ease the worries among Lib Dem MPs about the lack of a coherent vision for the party.
Davey says 'change to nature of politics itself' is needed
Davey said politics is broken.
But Conference, there is a bigger, more fundamental change we need to talk about.
A change to the nature of politics itself.
Because the things that have gone wrong in our country, the crises we face – the maternity crisis, the housing shortage, the sewage scandal, the cost of living, the sense that nothing quite works the way it should –
These are not the failings of the British people. Not for one second.
These are the failings of governments. Labour governments. Conservative governments. SNP governments in Holyrood.
